content: 1. Lactic acidosis and severe hepatomegaly with steatosis, including fatal cases, have been reported in patients treated with nucleoside analogues, either alone or in combination, such as stavudine and other antiretrovirals. 2. Although the relative rates of lactic acidosis have not been assessed in prospective, well-controlled trials, longitudinal cohort and retrospective studies suggest that this rare event may occur more frequently with antiretroviral regimens containing stavudine. 3. Risk factors for lactic acidosis may include female gender, obesity, and prolonged exposure to nucleoside analogues. 4. Fatal lactic acidosis has been reported in pregnant women receiving stavudine and didanosine in combination with other antiretroviral agents. 5. The combination of stavudine and didanosine should be used with caution during pregnancy and only if the potential benefits clearly outweigh the risks. 6. Particular caution is advised when administering stavudine to patients with known risk factors for liver disease; however, lactic acidosis has also been reported in patients without known risk factors. 7. Symptoms such as generalized fatigue, digestive issues (nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, unexplained weight loss), respiratory symptoms (tachypnea, dyspnea), or neurologic symptoms (including motor weakness) may indicate the development of symptomatic hyperlactatemia or lactic acidosis syndrome. 8. Treatment with stavudine should be suspended in patients who develop clinical or laboratory findings suggestive of symptomatic hyperlactatemia, lactic acidosis, or significant hepatotoxicity (including hepatomegaly and steatosis, even in the absence of marked transaminase elevations). 9. Permanent discontinuation of stavudine should be considered in patients with confirmed lactic acidosis. 10. The safety and efficacy of stavudine have not been established in HIV-infected patients with significant underlying liver disease. 11. Patients with preexisting liver dysfunction, including chronic active hepatitis, have an increased risk of liver function abnormalities, including severe and potentially fatal hepatic adverse events, during combination antiretroviral therapy. These patients should be monitored according to standard clinical practice. 12. If there is evidence of worsening liver disease, treatment interruption or discontinuation must be considered. 13. Hepatotoxicity and hepatic failure resulting in death have been reported during postmarketing surveillance in HIV-infected patients treated with hydroxyurea and other antiretroviral agents. 14. Fatal hepatic events were most frequently reported in patients treated with the combination of hydroxyurea, didanosine, and stavudine. This combination should be avoided. 15. In vitro studies have shown that ribavirin can reduce the phosphorylation of pyrimidine nucleoside analogues such as stavudine. 16. Although no pharmacokinetic or pharmacodynamic interactions (e.g., loss of HIV-1/HCV virologic suppression) were observed when ribavirin was coadministered with stavudine in HIV-1/HCV co-infected patients, hepatic decompensation (some fatal) has occurred in such patients receiving combination antiretroviral therapy for HIV-1 and interferon with or without ribavirin. 17. Patients receiving interferon with or without ribavirin and stavudine should be closely monitored for treatment-associated toxicities, particularly hepatic decompensation. 18. Discontinuation of stavudine should be considered as medically appropriate. Dose reduction or discontinuation of interferon, ribavirin, or both should also be considered if worsening clinical toxicities, including hepatic decompensation (e.g., Child-Pugh >6), are observed. 19. Motor weakness has been rarely reported in patients receiving combination antiretroviral therapy, including stavudine. Most cases occurred in the context of lactic acidosis. 20. The progression of motor weakness may mimic the clinical presentation of Guillain-Barré syndrome, including respiratory failure. If motor weakness develops, stavudine should be discontinued. Symptoms may persist or worsen even after discontinuation of therapy. 21. Peripheral sensory neuropathy, characterized by numbness, tingling, or pain in the hands or feet, has been reported in patients receiving stavudine therapy. 22. Peripheral neuropathy, which can be severe, is dose-related and occurs more frequently in patients with advanced HIV-1 disease, a history of peripheral neuropathy, or those receiving other drugs associated with neuropathy, including didanosine. 23. Patients should be monitored for the development of peripheral neuropathy. Stavudine-related peripheral neuropathy may resolve if therapy is promptly withdrawn. 24. If peripheral neuropathy develops, permanent discontinuation of stavudine should be considered. In some cases, symptoms may temporarily worsen after discontinuation of therapy. 25. Fatal and nonfatal pancreatitis have occurred during therapy when stavudine was part of a combination regimen that included didanosine, regardless of the degree of immunosuppression. 26. The combination of stavudine and didanosine, as well as any other agents toxic to the pancreas, should be suspended in patients with suspected pancreatitis. 27. Reintroduction of stavudine after a confirmed diagnosis of pancreatitis should be undertaken with extreme caution and close patient monitoring. The use of stavudine in combination with didanosine should be avoided. 28. Redistribution or accumulation of body fat, including central obesity, dorsocervical fat enlargement (buffalo hump), peripheral wasting, facial wasting, breast enlargement, and a Cushingoid appearance, has been observed in patients receiving antiretroviral therapy. 29. In randomized controlled trials of treatment-naive patients, clinical lipoatrophy or lipodystrophy developed in a higher proportion of patients treated with stavudine compared to other nucleosides (tenofovir or abacavir). 30. Dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DEXA) scans demonstrated overall limb fat loss in stavudine-treated patients compared to limb fat gain or no gain in patients treated with other nucleosides (abacavir, tenofovir, or zidovudine). 31. The incidence and severity of lipoatrophy or lipodystrophy are cumulative over time with stavudine-containing regimens. 32. In clinical trials, switching from stavudine to other nucleosides (tenofovir or abacavir) resulted in increases in limb fat with modest to no improvements in clinical lipoatrophy. 33. Patients receiving stavudine should be monitored for symptoms or signs of lipoatrophy or lipodystrophy and questioned about body changes related to these conditions. 34. Given the potential risks of stavudine, including lipoatrophy or lipodystrophy, a benefit-risk assessment should be conducted for each patient, and alternative antiretroviral therapy should be considered. 35. Immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome has been reported in patients treated with combination antiretroviral therapy, including stavudine. 36. During the initial phase of combination antiretroviral treatment, patients with an immune response may develop an inflammatory reaction to indolent or residual opportunistic infections (e.g., Mycobacterium avium infection, cytomegalovirus, Pneumocystis jiroveci pneumonia, or tuberculosis), which may require further evaluation and treatment. 37. Autoimmune disorders (e.g., Graves’ disease, polymyositis, Guillain-Barré syndrome) have also been reported in the context of immune reconstitution; however, the time to onset is more variable and can occur many months after initiating treatment.
